list.name: ds
list.label: Datasource
list.description: Which Prometheus scrapes Trench. Every panel follows this, so one dashboard serves dev, the Pi and production.

list.name: job
list.label: Job
list.description: Prometheus scrape job. trench_build_info is the probe because it is the one series every Trench emits unconditionally.

list.name: instance
list.label: Instance
list.description: Resolver instances inside the selected job. Leave on All to see the fleet; pick one to attribute a regression to a host.

list.name: action
list.label: Action
list.description: Outcome vocabulary: blocked, cached, forwarded, failed, authoritative, refused, ratelimited, rewrite, safesearch.

list.name: upstream
list.label: Upstream
list.description: Upstream resolvers that have answered. The exporter caps this at the 64 busiest, so a quiet upstream can be absent rather than idle.

list.name: qtype
list.label: Query type
list.description: DNS record types seen in questions.

list.name: win
list.label: Slow window
list.description: Averaging window for panels where a 1-minute rate is too noisy to read — detections, prefetch failures, eviction pressure.

list.name: slo_le
list.label: Latency SLO bucket
list.description: The histogram bucket that defines 'fast'. Only these values exist — they are LATENCY_BOUNDS_US from trench/stats/counters.py converted to seconds. Any other number silently matches nothing.

list.name: slo_target
list.label: SLO target
list.description: Share of queries that must land inside the SLO bucket. Drives the gauge thresholds and the error-budget panel.

list.name: topk
list.label: Top-K
list.description: How many series the top-N panels keep.

options.content:
# Trench — Full Telemetry

Every series `/metrics` exports, on one page. Panels are grouped by the question
they answer, not by the metric they happen to use.

**Start here:** *Golden signals* tells you whether the resolver is healthy.
*Latency* and *Cache & replay* tell you why it is fast or slow.
*Filtering & security* tells you what it is deciding. *Fleet* and *Process*
tell you whether the box underneath it is coping.

Hover any panel's **ⓘ** for what its query actually measures and how it can lie.

panels.title: Build
panels.description: `trench_build_info` is a constant 1 carrying the version as a label — the standard info-metric pattern. Two values here means a partially rolled-out fleet.

panels.title: Scrape
panels.description: Prometheus' own `up`. Zero here means every panel on this page is showing you the past, not the present — check this before you believe a sudden drop anywhere else.

panels.title: Golden signals — is the resolver healthy?
Throughput
panels.description: `rate(trench_queries_total)`. This is the denominator for almost every ratio on this dashboard; if it collapses, the ratios get noisy long before they get wrong.

panels.title: Blocked
panels.description: Share of queries the filter refused. There is no correct value — what matters is that it is *stable*. A step change without a list update is the signature of a new device or a new app, and a fall to zero usually means filtering was paused, not that the traffic got clean (check the state timeline to the right).

panels.title: Cache hit
panels.description: hits / (hits + misses). `shared_hits` is deliberately excluded: it is counted on a different path in trench/cache/cache.py and folding it in double-counts. It has its own panel in Cache & replay.

panels.title: Replay
panels.description: Share of answers served from a wire-resident recorded reply. A low number is not a fault — it means traffic is diverse, or a feature that makes replies client-specific is on. Read it next to *Replay permitted*: low-while-permitted is diversity, low-while-not-permitted is a config decision.

panels.title: p99 latency
panels.description: p99 over the whole process lifetime histogram, rated over the dashboard window. Bucket resolution is coarse above 1s (1 → 2.5 → +Inf), so a p99 reported as 2.5s means 'somewhere past one second' — do not read precision into the tail.

panels.title: Failures
panels.description: Queries that produced no usable answer. Distinct from SERVFAIL returned by an upstream — see *Response codes* — because a failure here is Trench's own verdict after every upstream was tried.

panels.title: Clients
panels.description: Distinct clients **since process start** — a cumulative gauge, not a current count. It only ever goes up, and it resets on restart; the step at a restart is not a device leaving.

panels.title: Uptime
panels.description: Lowest uptime across the selection, so a single restarted instance is visible in a fleet view. Restarts are also drawn as red annotations on every timeseries.

panels.title: Latency SLO attainment
panels.description: Share of queries answered within the **$slo_le s** bucket, against a target of **$slo_target**. This is a true histogram ratio, not an interpolated quantile, so it is exact — but only at bucket boundaries, which is why the bucket is a dropdown rather than a free-text millisecond value.

panels.title: Traffic by action
panels.description: The full outcome vocabulary, ranked. `rewrite`, `safesearch`, `authoritative` and `ratelimited` only appear once those features have fired at least once — an absent bar means never used, not zero rate.

panels.title: Service state
panels.description: The three switches that change what every other panel means. A block-ratio drop with `filtering paused` amber underneath it is not a traffic change. A replay ratio of zero with `replay permitted` off is a configuration decision, not a regression.

panels.title: Queries by outcome
panels.description: Stacked, so the top of the stack is total throughput and each band is its contribution. Colours are fixed per action across this whole dashboard — red is always blocked, green always cached, blue always forwarded.

panels.title: Outcome share
panels.description: Share over the *whole selected time range* (`$__range`), not the last scrape — so zooming the time picker changes this panel's meaning on purpose.

panels.title: Latency quantiles
panels.description: Quantiles are interpolated inside a bucket, so they inherit the bucket edges: 100µs, 500µs, 1ms, 2.5ms, 5ms, 10ms, 25ms, 50ms, 100ms, 250ms, 500ms, 1s, 2.5s. The mean is drawn dashed as a control — mean far below p99 is the normal shape for a resolver (cache hits dominate); mean tracking p99 means the cache stopped helping. A log y-axis is on because these span four decades.

panels.title: Latency distribution
panels.description: The histogram itself, not a summary of it. Bimodality is the thing to look for: a bright band low down (cache and replay hits) plus a second band high up (upstream resolution). One band drifting upward is a slow upstream; the low band fading is the cache losing its grip.

panels.title: Latency CDF over the window
panels.description: Cumulative share of queries answered at or below each bucket edge, over the selected range. Read it left to right and stop where it reaches your target — that bucket is the honest value for the SLO dropdown. `+Inf` is excluded so the bucket labels sort correctly as strings.

panels.title: SLO attainment vs target
panels.description: Attainment against a flat target line. The target is a scalar expression built from the dropdown, which is why it renders as a real series you can hover rather than a static threshold.

panels.title: Error-budget burn rate
panels.description: How fast the latency error budget is being spent, in multiples of the sustainable rate. 1 means you will exactly exhaust the budget over the period; 14.4 is the usual fast-burn page threshold. Below 1 the budget is refilling.

panels.title: Cache & replay — why it is fast
Cache events
panels.description: All six counters from the cache: hits, shared_hits, stale_hits, misses, stores, evictions. Stores climbing while hits stay flat means the working set does not fit. Evictions arriving in bursts rather than steadily means pressure, not turnover.

panels.title: Stale answers served
panels.description: Serve-stale is a availability feature and a correctness risk at the same time: every stale answer is one the authority has not confirmed. A few percent during an upstream wobble is the feature working. A sustained double-digit share means stale is load-bearing, which is a different system than the one you designed. Share is on the left axis, absolute rate on the right.

panels.title: Cache and index size
panels.description: The three things that own memory. On a constrained host this is the panel that explains an OOM: blocklist rules is a step function that moves only on a list refresh, while cache and replay entries breathe with traffic. Blocklist size is on the right axis because it is orders of magnitude larger.

panels.title: Replay (wire-resident fast path)
panels.description: Recordings are the cost, hits are the return. *Hits per recording* (right axis) is the efficiency number: below 1 the fast path is storing replies nothing asks for twice, which buys memory pressure and no latency. Compare against prefetch below — a busy fast path can starve prefetch of the misses it needs to learn from.

panels.title: Prefetch
panels.description: Entries refreshed before expiry, averaged over **$win** because prefetch is bursty by design and a 1-minute rate is unreadable. A rising failure ratio is an early warning that survives in the cache: those refreshes are the ones that would otherwise have become client-visible misses a minute later.

panels.title: Cache, replay and prefetch — window totals
panels.description: Absolute counts over the selected range, for the moments when a rate is the wrong unit — capacity planning, or answering 'how many stale answers did we actually serve during the incident'. Columns are renamed and reordered by transformations, not by query aliasing, so the raw data stays inspectable.

panels.title: Answers by upstream
panels.description: One band per upstream. The label carries the full transport string, so DoT and plain UDP to the same address are separate series — which is the point, because they fail differently. Note the exporter only emits the 64 busiest upstreams.

panels.title: Upstream share
panels.description: Distribution over the selected range. A policy that claims to pick the fastest upstream and a pie that is one solid colour are telling you the selection collapsed to a single server.

panels.title: Top $topk upstreams
panels.description: Ranked, ignoring the upstream dropdown on purpose — this panel answers 'who is actually carrying the load' even while the rest of the row is filtered to one server.

panels.title: $upstream
panels.description: This panel is **repeated once per selected upstream**. Select several in the Upstream dropdown to get a small-multiples wall where a single server going quiet is obvious at a glance — the thing a stacked chart hides.

panels.title: Upstream detail
panels.description: Rate now, total over the range, and share of the range — joined on the upstream label. The share column is a gauge cell so the table reads as a chart; the header filter is on, so you can pin this to one transport while the graphs above stay global.

panels.title: Filtering & security — what it is deciding
Blocked rate vs index size
panels.description: Put a list refresh next to its effect. The step in *rules in index* is the refresh; if the blocked rate does not move with it, the new rules match nothing this network asks for. The exported `trench_block_ratio` gauge is drawn too — it is a process-lifetime average, so it should lag the rate, and if it instead tracks it exactly something is resetting.

panels.title: Behavioural detections
panels.description: DGA and tunnelling detections, averaged over **$win**. These are *detections*, not blocks — a lexical DGA score cannot tell WiFi calling apart from malware on its own, so treat a spike as a prompt to open the query log, not as an incident. The absolute counts are on hidden query B; unhide it in edit mode when you need them.

panels.title: Response codes
panels.description: What clients were actually told. NXDOMAIN rising with blocked traffic is normal if the block mode is NXDOMAIN; SERVFAIL rising is an upstream or DNSSEC problem and should move together with the failure stat at the top of the page.

panels.title: Query types
panels.description: Record types in questions, top $topk. This is the panel that spots a client doing something odd — a flood of TXT or NULL is the shape of tunnelling, a sudden PTR wall is usually a scanner or a monitoring agent that just got installed.

panels.title: Response code detail
panels.description: Every rcode seen in the range with its share. The footer sums the count column, so it doubles as a check that the rcode breakdown adds up to total queries.

panels.title: Filtering switches
panels.description: Per-instance switch history, one cell per scrape bucket. Where the state timeline at the top merges runs to show you shape, this keeps every sample — use it to find the exact bucket a pause started in a fleet.

panels.title: Clients seen (cumulative)
panels.description: Monotonic since start. The useful reading is the *slope*, not the value: a flat line means no new devices, a staircase means something is churning source addresses — a privacy extension, a VPN, or a client that rotates.

panels.title: New clients per minute
panels.description: The derivative of the panel to the left, over **$win**. `rate()` on a gauge is not textbook, but this gauge only ever increases within a process life, so it behaves like a counter — and rate() handles the restart reset correctly, which `deriv()` would not.

panels.title: Queries per client
panels.description: Throughput normalised by population — the number that stays comparable when the network grows. A jump here with a flat client count is one device getting chatty, which is exactly what the console's query log is for.

panels.title: Per-instance throughput
panels.description: Load distribution across the fleet. Two instances behind one address should be roughly equal; a persistent split is a client pinning to whichever it learned first, not a balancing bug.

panels.title: p99 by instance
panels.description: Tail latency attributed per host. One instance with a worse p99 than its peers under the same load is a host problem — thermal throttling, a slow disk, a noisy neighbour — not a resolver problem, and no panel sourced from `/metrics` can prove that. Pair this dashboard with node_exporter.

panels.title: Uptime
panels.description: A sawtooth here is a restart loop. Each drop also fires the red *Restarts* annotation on every timeseries in this dashboard.

panels.title: Build info
panels.description: One row per instance with its version label promoted to a column. During a rollout this is the fastest way to see which hosts are on which build — and to know whether a metric that suddenly appeared is new code or new traffic.

panels.title: Scrape cost
panels.description: Prometheus' own view of `/metrics`. Sample count grows with upstream and rcode cardinality — the exporter caps upstreams at 64 for exactly this reason, so a sample count that climbs without bound means a label vocabulary escaped its cap.

panels.title: Exported series
panels.description: Total trench_* series in the datasource for this selection. Compare against the inventory below: a number far under it means a subsystem is not wired in (fast path and pipeline metrics are only emitted when those objects exist).

panels.title: Metric families
panels.description: Distinct trench_* metric names. The exporter defines 25 families including the three histogram children; anything less means an optional subsystem is absent.

panels.title: Counter resets
panels.description: How many times the query counter went backwards in **$win**. Any non-zero value is a process restart; sustained non-zero is a crash loop, and every ratio on this dashboard is unreliable while it lasts.

panels.title: Reference — metric inventory, coverage, alert rules

options.content:
### Metric inventory — every family `trench/ops/metrics.py` emits

| Metric | Type | Labels | Shown on |
|---|---|---|---|
| `trench_build_info` | gauge | `version` | Build, Build info, Version annotation |
| `trench_queries_total` | counter | — | Throughput, Queries per client, Per-instance, Counter resets |
| `trench_query_actions_total` | counter | `action` | Traffic by action, Queries by outcome, Outcome share, Failures |
| `trench_query_types_total` | counter | `type` | Query types |
| `trench_blocked_total` | counter | — | Blocked, Blocked rate vs index size |
| `trench_block_ratio` | gauge | — | Blocked rate vs index size (control series) |
| `trench_cache_size` | gauge | — | Cache and index size |
| `trench_cache_events_total` | counter | `event` | Cache events, Cache hit, Stale answers, Window totals |
| `trench_blocklist_size` | gauge | — | Cache and index size, Blocked rate vs index size |
| `trench_query_rcodes_total` | counter | `rcode` | Response codes, Response code detail |
| `trench_upstream_answers_total` | counter | `upstream` | Answers by upstream, Share, Top-K, Detail, per-upstream repeat |
| `trench_clients_seen` | gauge | — | Clients, Clients seen, New clients, Queries per client |
| `trench_detections_total` | counter | `kind` | Behavioural detections |
| `trench_query_duration_seconds` | histogram | `le` | Quantiles, Heatmap, CDF, SLO gauge, Burn rate, p99 by instance |
| `trench_avg_latency_ms` | gauge | — | *(see note)* |
| `trench_fastpath_total` | counter | `event` | Replay, Replay ratio, Window totals |
| `trench_fastpath_entries` | gauge | — | Cache and index size |
| `trench_fastpath_usable` | gauge | — | Service state, Filtering switches, Replay annotation |
| `trench_prefetch_total` | counter | `event` | Prefetch, Window totals |
| `trench_filtering_enabled` | gauge | — | Service state, Filtering switches |
| `trench_filtering_paused` | gauge | — | Service state, Filtering switches, Pause annotation |
| `trench_uptime_seconds` | gauge | — | Uptime, Restarts annotation, Counter resets |

**`trench_avg_latency_ms` is deliberately not given a panel of its own.** It is a
mean over the whole process life; it cannot show a regression that a p99 shows,
and putting it next to the quantiles invites someone to read it as a current
value. The histogram's own mean is drawn on *Latency quantiles* instead, rated
over the dashboard window, which is the honest version of the same idea.

### What this dashboard cannot show you

`/metrics` exposes exactly four pieces of configuration — the version, the
global filtering switch, the pause switch, and whether replay is permitted.
Everything else in `trench.yaml` (upstream policy, list selection, privacy
level, per-client groups, rate limits, DNSSEC mode, retention) is **not
exported**, so no Grafana panel can render it. Two honest ways to close that:

1. Export the config surface as info-gauges (`trench_config_info{key,value}` or
   one gauge per boolean) and add a table here. Cheap, and it makes settings
   changes graphable and alertable.
2. Point a JSON datasource (Infinity) at the console's `/api/v1/settings` and
   render it as a table. No resolver change, but it needs a plugin and a token.

Anything else on this page that claims to show a setting would be inventing it.

### Host metrics are a separate dashboard, on purpose

Nothing here can see CPU, memory, thermal throttling, or disk pressure — the
failure modes that actually kill a resolver on a small box. Run `node_exporter`
alongside and import **Node Exporter Full (ID 1860)** unmodified. Keeping "is
Trench healthy" and "is the host healthy" apart is what lets you tell them
apart.

### Ready-to-paste Prometheus rules

Recording rules first — every quantile panel here recomputes the same
aggregation, and on a constrained Prometheus that is the expensive part.

```yaml
groups:
  - name: trench-recording
    interval: 30s
    rules:
      - record: job_instance:trench_queries:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job, instance) (rate(trench_queries_total[5m]))
      - record: job_instance:trench_latency_seconds:p99
        expr: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (job, instance, le)
              (rate(trench_query_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))
      - record: job_instance:trench_cache_hit:ratio5m
        expr: sum by (job, instance) (rate(trench_cache_events_total{event="hits"}[5m]))
              / clamp_min(sum by (job, instance)
              (rate(trench_cache_events_total{event=~"hits|misses"}[5m])), 0.001)

  - name: trench-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: TrenchDown
        expr: up{job=~"trench.*"} == 0
        for: 2m
        labels: {severity: critical}
        annotations:
          summary: "Trench {{ $labels.instance }} is not being scraped"
          description: "Every DNS client behind this resolver is affected."

      - alert: TrenchNoTraffic
        expr: job_instance:trench_queries:rate5m == 0
        for: 10m
        labels: {severity: critical}
        annotations:
          summary: "Trench {{ $labels.instance }} is up but answering nothing"

      - alert: TrenchTailLatency
        expr: job_instance:trench_latency_seconds:p99 > 0.25
        for: 15m
        labels: {severity: warning}
        annotations:
          summary: "p99 above 250ms for 15m on {{ $labels.instance }}"

      - alert: TrenchFailureRate
        expr: sum by (job, instance)
              (rate(trench_query_actions_total{action="failed"}[5m]))
              / clamp_min(job_instance:trench_queries:rate5m, 0.001) > 0.02
        for: 10m
        labels: {severity: warning}

      - alert: TrenchServingStale
        expr: sum by (job, instance)
              (rate(trench_cache_events_total{event="stale_hits"}[5m]))
              / clamp_min(sum by (job, instance)
              (rate(trench_cache_events_total{event=~"hits|stale_hits|misses"}[5m])), 0.001) > 0.1
        for: 15m
        labels: {severity: warning}
        annotations:
          summary: "Over 10% of answers are stale on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Serve-stale has stopped being a safety net and become the path."

      - alert: TrenchFilteringPaused
        expr: trench_filtering_paused == 1
        for: 1h
        labels: {severity: warning}
        annotations:
          summary: "Filtering has been paused for an hour on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "A timed pause that outlives its reason is an open resolver."

      - alert: TrenchFilteringDisabled
        expr: trench_filtering_enabled == 0
        for: 15m
        labels: {severity: warning}

      - alert: TrenchBlocklistEmpty
        expr: trench_blocklist_size < 1000
        for: 15m
        labels: {severity: critical}
        annotations:
          summary: "Blocklist index collapsed on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "A failed list refresh leaves an index that loads and matches nothing."

      - alert: TrenchPrefetchFailing
        expr: sum by (job, instance) (rate(trench_prefetch_total{event="failed"}[15m]))
              / clamp_min(sum by (job, instance)
              (rate(trench_prefetch_total{event="issued"}[15m])), 0.001) > 0.25
        for: 30m
        labels: {severity: info}

      - alert: TrenchRestartLoop
        expr: resets(trench_uptime_seconds[15m]) > 2
        labels: {severity: critical}

      - alert: TrenchVersionSkew
        expr: count by (job) (count by (job, version) (trench_build_info)) > 1
        for: 1h
        labels: {severity: info}
        annotations:
          summary: "More than one Trench build is live in {{ $labels.job }}"
```

`TrenchBlocklistEmpty` is the one worth having even if you take nothing else:
a list refresh that fails open is silent — throughput, latency and error rates
all stay perfect while the filter matches nothing.

panels.title: Firing now
panels.description: Unified-alerting view filtered to this dashboard's tag. Rules come from the panel to the left once you load them into Prometheus or recreate them as Grafana rules.

panels.title: Related dashboards
panels.description: The compact Trench dashboard, plus anything else tagged `trench` or `dns`. Add your Node Exporter board to the tag and it shows up here.

panels.title: Resolution pipeline
panels.description: A canvas panel with each box bound to a named field, so the pipeline diagram carries live numbers. The binding depends on the reduce+merge transformations below producing one row whose columns are named by the query legends — if your Grafana version names them differently the boxes go blank but the diagram still renders. Every value is queries/s.

panels.title: Throughput vs tail latency
panels.description: Each point is one time bucket: throughput on x, p99 on y. A flat cloud means latency is independent of load — the resolver has headroom. An upward hook on the right is the saturation knee, and its x position is your real capacity number. This is the one question a timeseries genuinely cannot answer.
